source.title: Explicit Regularization via Regularizer Mirror Descent
source.authors: Navid Azizan; Sahin Lale; B. Hassibi

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; the supplied text ends after Appendix C results.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares explicit regularization methods with SGD and reports training and held-out accuracy under label corruption, bearing on overfitting and the training–test gap with a different intervention and task setup.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results for RMD, SGD, and weight decay across corruption levels and regularization strengths. Cited results and background claims are not extracted as rows. Exact table entries are retained where they quantify the comparisons.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates RMD regularization against SGD and weight decay, rather than testing V1–V8. Its SGD experiments fit partially corrupted labels and generalize on clean test data, but do not compare fully random-label training with natural-label training or measure chance-level generalization after fully random-label training as V1 specifies. Implicit regularization and interpolation provide background motivation.
record.authors_conclusion: The record broadly captures the empirical conclusion, but should qualify the advantage: RMD substantially improves peak test accuracy at 25% and 40% label randomization, improves it only marginally at 10%, and loses to SGD on clean data. The authors claim more predictable parameter sensitivity than weight decay and prove convergence near a regularized minimizer under assumptions. Their continual-learning contribution is a mathematical extension, without a continual-learning experiment.
record.recipe_differences: The study introduces RMD, an explicit regularization method evaluated on ResNet-18 with CIFAR-10 label corruption. It does not reproduce any of the listed original methods or claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Test accuracy varies with label corruption and regularization strength λ. The authors describe weight-decay test accuracy as erratic and sensitive to λ; RMD performance is more consistent, though at larger λ it approaches SGD.

fits_no_version.finding: On ResNet-18 with CIFAR-10, peak RMD test accuracy is 83.63% versus SGD's 67.41% at 40% label randomization, 86.92% versus 79.42% at 25%, and 88.49% versus 87.87% at 10%. Some RMD settings perform worse than SGD. On clean data, SGD reaches 92.81%, exceeding all reported RMD and weight-decay settings.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: RMD can improve generalization under partial training-label corruption in this setup, with benefits depending on corruption level and regularization strength.

record.problems: Experiments are limited to one architecture and CIFAR-10; uncertainty estimates are not reported. The learning rates are selected from a small set, and results are presented for the best-performing choices. The authors note that different weight-decay runs with the same hyperparameters can have drastically different test accuracies.
record.rows_left_out: The 60-row limit is reached at Table 3. Omitted remaining Table 3 rows for RMD λ=1.6 through 16.0 and weight-decay λ=0.001 through 0.006, and all Table 4 results for uncorrupted CIFAR-10. These results are summarized in Appendix C.3–C.4; Table 4 reports SGD at 100% training and 92.81% test accuracy, RMD test accuracy from 84.99% to 92.35%, and weight-decay test accuracy from 76.13% to 91.62%.

untested.parts: Paired natural-label and fully random-label training, including random-label held-out accuracy at chance. Partial corruption and clean-data interpolation do not establish this comparison.
Width-dependent test error beyond zero training error; no width sweep.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and the role of local connectivity; only ResNet-18 is evaluated.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning; neither Adam nor another adaptive comparator is evaluated.
Batch-size effects and recipe adaptations under fixed epoch budgets; batch size remains 128.
Dropout effects, underfitting, small-data regimes, and jointly removing dropout and weight decay; no dropout intervention.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its ranking of generalization gaps; no perturbation or measure-ranking experiment.
Removing highly memorized versus randomly selected examples and retraining; no such removal experiment.

record.verdict_notes: All recorded numerical pairs match the supplied tables. Corruption percentages denote labels selected for random reassignment; expected incorrect-label fractions are 36%, 22.5%, and 9%. Appendix B reports fixed crop/flip augmentation, different stopping criteria across algorithms, and learning rates selected from three choices. Appendix tables provide more precise values than the main-text summaries. Table 3 contradicts the narrative's consistently-better claim at lambda=1.5 and 1.6. Omitted table settings and clean-data results are already declared in rows_left_out and do not supply a missing V1–V8 test.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label memorization comparison or natural-label test accuracy comparison is reported.
No width sweep beyond the interpolation threshold is reported.
No convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparison is reported.
No adaptive optimizer comparison is reported.
No sharpness or generalization-measure comparison is reported.
No removal of memorized examples is reported.

relation.reason: The introduction discusses memorization capacity and generalization as motivation, while the study's own results evaluate RMD against SGD and weight decay.

tranche.reason: The experiments compare noisy-label regularization methods outside V1–V8. Partial label randomization with clean test labels does not establish V1's fully random-label comparison; the other versions' effects are not tested or used.

source_check.notes: Table 2 repeats lambda=1.6; R36 correctly preserves the second entry without establishing a replicate. Corruption percentages denote labels selected for random reassignment, not percentages necessarily assigned incorrect labels.
